moments.detail: The tool already stapled prompts and traces onto every commit, but a raw transcript is not context: you still had to read the whole thing to figure out why the code moved. moments.detail: The whole point was to pick up your own session on the other laptop, and it just wouldn't switch: machine A kept its stale copy and, for extra insult, pulling the full session froze the terminal. Turned out identity was tied to the machine, so laptop A and laptop B looked like two different people who happened to share a name. Once sessions were keyed on GitHub id plus name with a contributor set, the fetch could also be made cancellable, which is how the freeze finally became a thing you could press Esc on.

moments.detail: The rename itself was the boring part; the funny part is that the README screenshot kept betraying them. First it still had "agit" in the dashboard path, then it showed the full home directory of whoever took it, which is not something you want on a public intro page, so the fix became abbreviating repo paths to ~ and shooting it again. moments.summary: The project became aGiTrack everywhere, then packaged itself for publishing with pictures to prove it.

moments.detail: The complaint that started it was mundane: choosing exit sometimes sat there for thirty seconds with a vague "Finalizing commits..." message and no clue why. Turns out every git call was happening on the same thread that read your keystrokes, so runner.py got a dedicated git worker and the poll loop learned to back off when nobody had typed and no session was running, with the floor raised from 0.2s to a full second because polling five times a second to save battery is a joke that tells itself.
moments.summary: The terminal froze on every git call, so git got its own background thread and a sleep switch.

thoughts.note: The ask was pure laptop-owner pragmatism: if nothing is happening, stop burning the battery on it.
thoughts.quote: aGiTrack should pause background tasks/checks when the user didn't type into the aGiTrack terminal for some time and there is no active session running. This should save the battery. On Mac, it was saying that VS Studio is consuming significant energy when aGiTrack runs inside it; that warning was gone after quitting aGiTrack.

thoughts.note: Pushing back on the agent's own 0.2s interval, and on brute-force walking of every file and folder while they were at it.
thoughts.quote: ACTIVE_POLL_SECONDS (0.2s) sounds like a very small interval. No poll should be less than a second. Make sure that any file and folder checks are efficient too, instead of brute-forcelly checking though every file and folder. Only read parts of files and folders as needed. Use some list files function with last modified time if appropriate.

moments.detail: The want was simple and slightly greedy: what about all the work done before aGiTrack was watching, or in a directory that isn't even a git repo? Turns out the Claude and OpenCode transcripts already hold enough to rebuild it, so backtrace.py walks the session logs and reassembles turns into commit-shaped history. Then came the long tail of it being wrong in interesting ways: diffs that accumulated across turns instead of showing one turn's damage, and forked conversations counted twice, which made backtrace claim more AI lines than the dashboard thought existed in total.
moments.summary: The agent's own chat log turns out to be enough to reconstruct what happened, commit by commit.

thoughts.note: Setting the bar deliberately low on prerequisites: no git needed, just one session that touched files here.
thoughts.quote: Please note that this backtrace feature can run even if the directory is not a git repo. It only needs to require that there has been at least one session running that led to file changes in the current directory.

moments.detail: The whole thing started because in no-worktree mode aGiTrack kept popping the commit dialog for edits the user never made, and the first fix guessed authorship from where the file lived. moments.detail: The trigger was mundane: paste a few lines into the backend agent's terminal and aGiTrack read the embedded newlines as Enter, cheerfully answering its own "new commits arrived" popup on your behalf. Fixing that meant getting serious about who is allowed to act without being asked, which is how the same stretch of work ended up in agitrack/update/selfupdate.py and restart.py. Along the way the update feature briefly shipped opt-in, which prompted a fairly direct "it should be default on" and a config flag for the two people who disagree.
moments.summary: A paste bug led to self-update with multi-instance locking, so two copies never upgrade at once.

thoughts.note: Realizing the popup was consuming keystrokes that were never meant for it, just characters passing through on their way to the agent.
thoughts.quote: When pasting multiple lines into the backend agent's terminal, some line breaks in what is pasted gets detected by aGiTrack as Enter, which unintentionally gets applied to aGiTrack's pop up menu asking users about new commits etc. This should be avoided.

thoughts.note: Pushing back on the agent's cautious default: on by default, with an escape hatch, not the other way around.
thoughts.quote: What do you mean by self-updating is now opt-in? It should be default on although you can add a global config option for any user who wants to turn it off.

moments.detail: The complaint was simple: one panel in the dashboard still had its own scrollbar, so you'd scroll the page and the inner frame would just sit there smugly. Flattening it in web.py meant the "see example →" link from the homepage suddenly pointed at nothing, so the anchor into the static demo had to be re-aimed too. While in there, backtrace_commit.py stopped emitting the same backtrace twice, and the little vertical guide line on expanded commits got dropped because nobody asked for it.
moments.summary: One stubborn nested scroll area got flattened, and duplicate backtraces stopped showing up twice.

thoughts.note: Removing the nested scroll meant the homepage deep-link into the demo page had to move with it, so both got fixed in one pass.
thoughts.quote: There is still frame with separate scrolling in the currently running dashboard. Also, when you remove the separate scrolling, make sure the "see example →" from homepage links to the correct location in the static demo page.

moments.detail: The ask was simple enough: a third page next to the dashboard and the learn page, calling the agent backend to turn commits into a timeline you'd actually read. What followed was a long argument with the model about what a chapter is. It kept generating dozens of them, kept claiming Windows had just landed when Windows was a month old, and kept cutting the chain of thought off mid-word, so 'chapters' eventually got thrown out entirely and replaced with zoom levels in story.py.
moments.summary: A whole second web UI built in parallel, plus the TUI scrolling fix nobody asked for yet.

thoughts.note: Said the same thing twice in one go, which is what happens when the story page hands you thirty chapters again.
thoughts.quote: The story page is still broken. Every generation should only start with the latest few chapters. There could be a coarse story over the entire prject timeframe too. But there should be far less number of chapters shown to the user at once. Also once I start generating, the page keeps flashing and it's hard to stop. The animation is not shown properly.

thoughts.note: Caught the act summary bragging about Windows integration that had shipped a month earlier, which is a very specific way to notice your summarizer isn't reading dates.
thoughts.quote: Please continue with the 2 tasks first.
